data.title: Storage stocks strangle South Korean retail investors
data.description:
Author: Su Yang, Tencent Technology

The global memory chip market is experiencing an unprecedented price surge.

AI data centers are making massive purchases of memory chips, with Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology's production capacity being pre-booked. The price of some memory chips has increased tenfold in the past year. Electronics manufacturers are scrambling to find suppliers to secure supplies, and some products have even had to raise prices and reduce specifications.

While the supply chain is busy scrambling for supplies, the capital market is selling off memory stocks.

On November 25th local time, SK Hynix's stock price fell 11.05%, Samsung Electronics fell 9.87%, and the Korea Composite Stock Price Index (KOSPI) fell more than 6%. Storage stocks, which had previously benefited from the continued surge in AI demand, suddenly experienced a concentrated sell-off. On one hand, there is a shortage of chips, with manufacturers' orders booked for years to come; on the other hand, investors are worried that high profits are unsustainable. Institutions such as Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley have already turned their attention to 2028, assessing the potential changes in storage prices and corporate profits after the release of new production capacity. AI demand continues to drive up storage chip prices, but the stock market has already cooled down this boom cycle in advance. How long will the storage chip shortage last? The most direct driver of this storage shortage comes from AI data centers. Large technology companies are continuously building AI infrastructure, requiring the purchase of large quantities of DRAM and high-bandwidth memory (HBM). Compared to traditional consumer electronics customers, cloud computing giants have more funds and make larger purchases. To secure supply, they are willing to sign long-term contracts and even lock in capacity for the next few years in advance. SK Hynix is ​​one of the main beneficiaries of this demand growth. The company holds a significant market share in the HBM field, and the demand for high-bandwidth memory from AI chip manufacturers such as Nvidia has brought it a large number of orders. As AI servers continue to expand, storage manufacturers are facing increasingly tight capacity. SK Hynix's memory chips are installed on memory modules. The pressure from AI demand has also spread to the traditional memory market. Because HBM is more profitable, manufacturers are investing more production resources in this area. However, HBM manufacturing involves complex processes and packaging, and its production resources, equipment, and capital investment compete with traditional DRAM, thus squeezing out the general memory needed by consumer electronics manufacturers. Expanding production capacity also cannot quickly alleviate the shortage. While Samsung Electronics, SK Hynix, and Micron Technology are all increasing investment, building new wafer fabs requires significant time for construction, equipment installation, process debugging, and capacity ramp-up. It takes considerable time from initial investment to effective supply. A November 25th report in the Wall Street Journal stated that some electronics manufacturers have established dedicated teams to procure memory chips, even resorting to secondhand trading platforms like eBay to find inventory. Some companies have had to readjust their procurement plans to secure supplies from Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. The rising memory prices are also beginning to impact the consumer market. Apple has raised prices on some MacBooks, and the starting price of the iPhone 18 Pro series has increased; Microsoft's Xbox, Amazon's Echo Dot, and Meta Quest are also facing cost pressures. Some manufacturers have opted to reduce device memory configurations; Motorola has reduced the storage capacity of some models from 256GB to 128GB, without a corresponding price reduction. Some popular electronic products have seen price increases due to rising memory costs. However, demand is not growing in all sectors. A storage industry report released by GF Securities on November 26, citing TrendForce data, stated that Chinese cloud service providers have recently slowed their procurement pace, with insufficient GPU supply being one reason. Adjustments to related server DRAM orders account for approximately 1% of global DRAM demand, and procurement by US cloud service providers is expected to absorb this shortfall. The situation in the consumer market is even more noteworthy. Some customers have cut orders for enterprise-grade solid-state drives (eSSDs), and consumer electronics manufacturers have begun to reduce memory configurations, thus weakening demand for consumer-grade DRAM, with DDR4 being particularly affected. Guangfa Securities has consequently lowered its 2027 DRAM contract price forecast. Previously, the institution predicted that prices would rise by 10%, 7%, 5%, and 3% quarter-on-quarter in the four quarters of next year; the latest forecast has been lowered to 6%, 3%, 0%, and 0%. According to this forecast, DRAM prices will continue to rise in the first half of next year, and remain basically flat in the second half. However, the slowdown in price increases does not necessarily mean that supply is sufficient. Guangfa Securities still expects a supply gap of 5%, 5%, and 4% in the DRAM market from 2026 to 2028. HBM continues to occupy wafer capacity, and major manufacturers remain cautious about expanding traditional DRAM production, resulting in an overall tight supply. The shortage is also reflected in manufacturers' order cycles. SK Hynix has already sold its DRAM capacity up to 2029, and Micron has also secured a large supply in advance through multi-year contracts. SK Hynix CFO Kim Woo-hyun previously stated that the supply constraints may continue until 2030. However, there are differing opinions among institutions regarding how long the supply shortage will last. Nomura Securities believes that AI infrastructure construction will continue to support storage demand, and the supply shortage may continue until 2028. Goldman Sachs predicts that the DRAM supply-demand gap will narrow from 5.1% in 2027 to 1.2% in 2028, with traditional DRAM and NAND prices potentially falling by about 20% respectively. Stock Prices Diverge from Demand While memory chip prices are still rising, SK Hynix's stock price has already fallen sharply. Behind these two trends lies the different judgments of the industry's current demand and the capital market's assessment of future profitability. The memory industry has a clear cyclical nature. When supply is tight, manufacturers can raise prices, and profits increase accordingly; as new capacity is gradually released, the supply-demand relationship may reverse, and chip prices and profit margins will fall accordingly. This is precisely what investors are worried about. While SK Hynix benefits from HBM demand, its traditional DRAM and NAND businesses still impact its overall performance. Whether HBM business growth can fully offset this impact if traditional memory prices decline in the coming years remains uncertain. Guangfa Securities' calculations for 2028 demonstrate the potential downside for memory prices. Using a 2027 traditional DRAM price of $16 per GB as a benchmark, the firm calculated three scenarios: if prices return to pre-AI demand levels, they could fall to $4 per GB; based on long-term contract prices, approximately $8; and if demand remains strong, they could remain at $12. The corresponding declines are 75%, 50%, and 25%, respectively. HBM prices also have room to decline. Guangfa Securities predicts that the price per GB in 2028 may be between $20.7 and $29.6, 0% to 30% lower than the $29.6 in 2027. However, Guangfa Securities is not bearish on major storage manufacturers. The institution remains optimistic about Micron, SK Hynix, and Samsung Electronics, believing that if demand continues to weaken and prices begin to fall, major manufacturers may control supply by reducing production to prevent further price declines. Expectations for AI infrastructure investment have also seen significant adjustments recently. On November 26, research firm SemiAnalysis released a report that significantly lowered its forecasts for future AI computing power investment. The report projects that global AI accelerator capital expenditure will fall to $758 billion in 2028 from the previously forecast $1.04 trillion, a decrease of approximately 28%; chip spending in 2030 is projected to drop to $923 billion from $1.53 trillion, a decrease of 40%. The report also lowered its forecasts for chip shipments and energy demand. According to the latest forecasts, AI chip shipments between 2026 and 2030 will be 17% lower than previously expected, with HBM shipments expected to decline by 30%. South Korean brokerages have diverged in their market outlook. Daol Investment Securities believes that the recent stock price correction is too drastic relative to the company's fundamentals, maintaining a buy rating on SK Hynix with a fair value of 2 million won. BNK Investment & Securities lowered its target price to 1.05 million won, anticipating that customers and distributors will begin adjusting their inventories in the second and third quarters of next year, potentially leading to a significant drop in memory chip prices. Overseas investment banks are also lowering their forecasts. Goldman Sachs lowered its target price for SK Hynix from 3.5 million won to 2 million won, but maintained a buy rating. Morgan Stanley lowered its target price from 2.6 million won to 1.6 million won, warning of a potential "profit cliff" in 2028. Morgan Stanley also lowered its long-term average operating profit margin forecast for SK Hynix from 2029 to 2035 from 53% to 28%, reflecting its concerns about the long-term profitability of the memory industry. Not all institutions are bearish. Nomura Securities maintains its target price of 4.7 million won for SK Hynix, believing that the demand driven by AI infrastructure construction is sufficient to support supply shortages for an extended period. The core disagreement among institutions is not about whether AI still needs memory chips, but rather whether demand growth can continue to outpace supply expansion, and how long the high profits generated during the shortage period can be sustained. Stock prices have already begun to reflect these concerns, but the current shortage situation in the industry remains unchanged. Who is facing margin calls? The sharp fluctuations in memory stocks have also caused heavy losses for South Korean leveraged investors who bet on an upward trend. On November 25th, several SK Hynix single-stock leveraged ETFs in the South Korean market fell by more than 21%. The RISE SK Hynix single-stock leveraged ETF fell 22.78%, the KIWOOM SK Hynix Futures Single-Stock Leveraged ETF fell 22.21%, and similar products under SOL and KODEX fell 21.84% and 21.72% respectively. This is not the first time South Korean retail investors have suffered heavy losses in leveraged trading of storage stocks. According to data submitted to the National Assembly by the Financial Supervisory Service of Korea, from May 27th, when single-stock leveraged products were launched, to August 14th, individual investors suffered cumulative losses of 6.313 trillion won on single-stock leveraged and inverse products related to Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. Of this, realized losses amounted to 2.3242 trillion won, while unsold products showed a paper loss of 3.9888 trillion won. Investors of all ages were affected. Investors in their 40s suffered the largest cumulative losses, approximately 2.053 trillion won; those in their 50s suffered losses of approximately 1.8655 trillion won. Investors over 70 years old lost an average of approximately 29.94 million won per account. The drawdowns of individual products were even more dramatic. South Korean financial media outlet Edaily reported on November 6 that the SOL SK Hynix single-stock leveraged ETF closed at 3,340 won that day, a drop of approximately 91% from its high point on June 22. A similar product on KODEX fell from 44,000 won to around 4,000 won, also a drop of over 90%. The TIGER product experienced a similar decline. South Korean media had previously reported that some retail investors continued to buy leveraged products during the decline in storage stocks, hoping to lower their average cost and wait for a rebound. The concentrated sell-off on November 25 inflicted even greater losses on these investors.

data.title: Stablecoin Critic Set To Lead ECB As Europe's Digital Currency Battle Intensifies
data.description:
Stablecoin Critic Hernández de Cos Set to Replace Lagarde as ECB President

Hernández de Cos, a former governor of Spain's central bank, has secured the backing of eurozone governments to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president after the Netherlands withdrew its support for rival candidate Klaas Knot, a former governor of the Dutch central bank.

🇪🇺 LATEST: Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos has been picked by eurozone countries to succeed Christine Lagarde as ECB president when she steps down on Feb. 7. https://t.co/BAMHU8K1ZS

— Cointelegraph (@Cointelegraph) November 27, 2026

The European Council put forward Hernández de Cos for the position on November 26, following the Council's recommendation. He is expected to take office on February 7, 2027, when Lagarde leaves the role, although the appointment still requires consultations with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council before a formal decision.

Congratulations to Pablo Hernandez de Cos for earning the support of the EU Council to become ECB’s next President, and to Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier for being recommended to join ECB’s Executive Board!

— Kristalina Georgieva (@KGeorgieva) November 26, 2026

His potential elevation comes with particular significance for the cryptocurrency industry, given his skepticism toward stablecoins and preference for alternative forms of digital money.

Hernández de Cos Questions Stablecoins' Viability for Mainstream Payments

Speaking at the Jackson Hole Economic Symposium in August, Hernández de Cos questioned whether stablecoins in their current form could become a credible means of payment at scale, arguing that tokenized bank deposits offer a more promising alternative for everyday transactions and wholesale settlement.

Pablo Hernández de Cos, un español al frente del Banco Central Europeo para dirigir la política monetaria de la eurozona. El relevo oficial se producirá tras la salida de Lagarde el 7 de febrero de 2027

— RTVE Noticias (@rtvenoticias) November 26, 2026

Although he acknowledged that stablecoins could serve specialized purposes, he warned that their widespread adoption could create broader risks for the traditional financial system.

In particular, he cautioned that growing reliance on US dollar-backed stablecoins outside the United States could undermine monetary sovereignty and weaken domestic monetary policy transmission. He also warned that a shift away from traditional bank deposits could increase banks' funding costs and potentially tighten lending conditions.

🔥 JUST IN: Tether has officially launched USA₮, a US-regulated, dollar-backed stablecoin built for the American market. https://t.co/i8hC7pHcDz

— Cointelegraph (@Cointelegraph) January 27, 2026

His position highlights the distinction between privately issued stablecoins and tokenized bank deposits, which represent commercial bank liabilities recorded on programmable digital platforms.

Rather than relying primarily on privately issued tokens, Hernández de Cos has argued for a monetary system that builds on tokenized deposits while preserving the role of central bank money in financial settlement.

Digital Euro Could Gain a Supporter as ECB Advances CBDC Plans

While Hernández de Cos has expressed reservations about stablecoins, he has been more receptive to central bank digital currencies (CBDCs), particularly the proposed digital euro.

In a 2023 speech, he argued that a digital euro could encourage innovation in payments while helping safeguard Europe's monetary sovereignty.

🇪🇺 BREAKING: The European Central Bank today published its Tokenisation Reference Model. The model serves as a framework for a single European tokenisation rulebook. https://t.co/wb1sB6m58A

— Generation Infinity (@Genfinity) November 24, 2026

His potential appointment comes as the ECB continues developing its digital euro initiative, with a pilot planned for 2027 and a potential launch in 2029, subject to legislative approval.

JUST IN: 🇪🇺 European Central Bank seeks partners to test tokenized bank deposits and securities.

— Watcher Guru (@WatcherGuru) November 21, 2026

This creates an interesting contrast between his position on privately issued stablecoins and his support for a central bank-backed digital currency.

If confirmed, Hernández de Cos would take charge of the ECB as it advances its plans to introduce the digital euro, placing him at the center of Europe's efforts to modernize its payment infrastructure.

ECB Appointment Still Awaits Final Approval

Despite securing political backing, Hernández de Cos has yet to receive his formal appointment as ECB president. The European Council will first consult the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council before making its final decision, which is expected in December.

Pablo Hernandez de Cos is set to become the next European Central Bank president, succeeding Christine Lagarde when she leaves her role early in February 2027. Zoe Schneeweiss explains https://t.co/hPJu0HWjxZ https://t.co/tMSHhk7XAJ

— Bloomberg (@business) November 26, 2026

The selection followed negotiations between eurozone governments over Lagarde's successor. The Netherlands had initially backed Knot, but withdrew its support as Hernández de Cos secured the necessary backing from member states.

Lagarde announced in October that she would leave the ECB presidency on February 7, 2027, nine months before the scheduled end of her eight-year term.

Once formally appointed, Hernández de Cos will serve an eight-year, non-renewable term, leading the ECB through an important period for European monetary policy and the development of its digital currency infrastructure.
